## Optimization Theory

`Colossus` offers three levels of score calculation: calculating only the score, calculating the score and first derivative, and calculating the score and both first and second derivatives. The second and third options correspond to the Gradient Descent and Newton-Raphson optimization approaches. The goal of this vignette is to discuss how these methods are different, and in what circumstances each might be most appropriate. In both cases, the algorithm is designed to iteratively change the parameter estimates to approach a set of parameter values that optimize the score. The major difference is how much information is being calculated and used.

The Newton-Raphson algorithm calculates the second derivative matrix, inverts it, and solves a linear system of equations to set the first derivative vector to zero. This method establishes both a magnitude and direction for every step. So every step has several time-intensive calculations, but the new parameter estimates are informed. In this algorithm, `Colossus` uses both a learning rate ($\eta$) and maximum allowable parameter change ($\beta_{max}$). `Colossus` uses half-steps to slowly reduce the allowable step size as the solution approaches the optimum.


<p class="text-center" style="background-color: aliceblue">
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \Delta \beta \cdot \frac{\partial^2 LL}{\partial \beta^2} \approx - \frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta} \\
    \Delta \beta = - \eta \frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta_{t}} \cdot \left ( \frac{\partial^2 LL}{\partial \beta_{t}^2} \right)^{-1} \\
    \beta_{t+1} = \beta_{t} + \frac{\Delta \beta}{\left | \Delta \beta \right |} \cdot \min \left( \left[ \left|\Delta \beta \right|, \beta_{\max} \right] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$
</p>

The alternative is a Gradient descent approach. In this algorithm, the first derivatives are calculated and used to determine the vector with the highest change in score. This establishes a direction for the change in parameters, which is multiplied by the learning rate ($\eta$). Similar to the Newton-Raphson algorithm, the magnitude is limited by a maximum allowable parameter change ($\beta_{max}$). The Gradient algorithm avoids the time-intensive second-derivative calculations but takes less informed steps. So each iteration runs faster, but more iterations may be required. In both cases, the best parameter set is recorded and returned.

<p class="text-center" style="background-color: aliceblue">
$$
\begin{aligned}
   \Delta \beta = \eta  \cdot  \frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta}\\
   \beta_{t+1} = \beta_{t} + \frac{\Delta \beta}{\left | \Delta \beta \right |} \cdot \min \left( \left[ \left|\Delta \beta \right|, \beta_{\max} \right] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$
</p>

The standard half-step framework is not likely to be sufficient for the Gradient descent algorithm. Because of this, several different optimization options have been added: momentum, adadelta, and adam. Each use previous information about the gradient to inform the step size for future steps.

The first method, momentum, applies a weighted sum ($\gamma$) of the current and the previous step. This is done to speed up steps moving toward the optimum position and correct for when the algorithm oversteps. This can avoid the issue of oscillation around an optimum value.

<p class="text-center" style="background-color: aliceblue">
$$
\begin{aligned}
   \Delta \beta_{t} = \eta  \cdot \left (\gamma  \cdot  \Delta \beta_{t-1} + \frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta} \right )\\
   \beta_{t+1} = \beta_{t} + \frac{\Delta \beta_t}{\left | \Delta \beta_t \right |} \cdot \min \left( \left[ \left|\Delta \beta_{t} \right|, \beta_{\max} \right] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$
</p>

The next method, the adadelta method, applies a parameter-specific learning rate by tracking the root mean square (RMS) gradient and parameter updates within a window. Instead of tracking a true window of iteration, the old estimate of RMS is decayed by a weight ($\gamma$) before being added to the new estimate. The ratio of RMS parameter update to RMS gradient is used to normalize the results back in the correct units. A small offset ($\epsilon$) is used to avoid the case of division by zero.

<p class="text-center" style="background-color: aliceblue">
$$
\begin{aligned}
    g_t = \left (\frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta} \right)_{t} \\
    E[g^2]_{t} = \gamma  \cdot  E[g^2]_{t-1} + (1-\gamma)  \cdot  g^2_{t} \\
    E[\Delta \beta^2]_{t-1} = \gamma  \cdot  E[\Delta \beta^2]_{t-2} + (1-\gamma)  \cdot  \Delta \beta^2_{t-1} \\
    RMS[g]_t = \sqrt{E[g^2]_{t} + \epsilon} \\
    RMS[\Delta \beta]_{t-1} = \sqrt{E[\Delta \beta^2]_{t-1} + \epsilon} \\
   \Delta \beta_{t} = \frac{RMS[\Delta \beta]_{t-1}}{RMS[g]_t}  \cdot  g_t\\
   \beta_{t+1} = \beta_{t} + \frac{\Delta \beta_t}{\left | \Delta \beta_t \right |} \cdot \min \left( \left[ \left|\Delta \beta_{t} \right|, \beta_{\max} \right] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$
</p>

The final method, adam, combines the theory behind the momentum and adadelta methods. The adam method tracks an estimate of the first moment vector ($m$) and second moment vector ($v$), which are weighted by decay parameters ($\alpha_1, \alpha_2$). These are bias corrected to correct for bias in early iterations ($\hat{m}, \hat{v}$). The learning rate ($\eta$) and second moment vector provide the decaying learning rate from adadelta, and the first moment vector provides an effect similar to momentum. Combined, these have generally been able to stabilize gradient descent algorithms without incurring a significant computational cost.

<p class="text-center" style="background-color: aliceblue">
$$
\begin{aligned}
    g_t = \left (\frac{\partial LL}{\partial \beta} \right)_{t} \\
    m_0, v_0 = 0, 0 \\
    m_t = \alpha_1  \cdot  m_{t-1} + (1-\alpha_1)  \cdot  g_t \\
    v_t = \alpha_2  \cdot  v_{t-1} + (1-\alpha_2)  \cdot  g^2_t \\
    \hat{m}_t = m_t / (1-\alpha_1^t) \\
    \hat{v}_t = v_t / (1-\alpha_2^t) \\
   \Delta \beta_{t} = \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}  \cdot  \hat{m}_t \\
   \beta_{t+1} = \beta_{t} + \frac{\Delta \beta_t}{\left | \Delta \beta_t \right |} \cdot \min \left( \left[ \left|\Delta \beta_{t} \right|, \beta_{\max} \right] \right)
\end{aligned}
$$
</p>


## Use in Practice

The first thing to acknowledge is that the gradient descent method may require more hyperparameter tuning than the standard Newton-Raphson method. In general, it may be necessary to run the analysis multiple times with different learning rates, decay terms, and offsets. The following test example shows the basic usage with a simple model, and are not tuned for performance. The functions were run previously and the results were recorded.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
fname <- "tests/testthat/ll_comp_0.csv"
colTypes <- c("double", "double", "double", "integer", "integer")
df <- fread(fname, nThread = 1, data.table = TRUE, header = TRUE, colClasses = colTypes, fill = TRUE)
set.seed(3742)
df$rand <- floor(runif(nrow(df), min = 0, max = 5))

keep_constant <- c(0, 0)

# Code not run due to duration
for (method in c("none", "momentum", "adadelta", "adam")) {
  gradient_control <- list()
  if (method != "none") {
    gradient_control[[method]] <- TRUE
  }
  a_n <- c(0.01, 0.01)
  control <- list(
    ncores = 1, lr = 0.2, maxiters = c(1, 50),
    halfmax = 2, epsilon = 1e-6, step_max = 0.5,
    deriv_epsilon = 1e-6, verbose = 4
  )
  e <- CoxRun(Cox(t0, t1, lung) ~ loglinear(dose, rand, 0) + m(), df,
    a_n = a_n, keep_constant = keep_constant,
    control = control, gradient_control = gradient_control
  )
  print(e)
}
```

Every gradient descent algorithm available was tested at the same starting point. In all cases, the algorithm approaches the solution at different rates. In this case, there are no local extrema, so the standard approach is fine. These show some fundamental differences between the methods. The standard and momentum approaches are both subject to oscillation over many iterations, while the adam and adadelta approaches tend to converge. The differences between adadelta and adam are also visible, the adam method converged quicker. However, these results did not necessarily use optimized hyperparameters and this is not meant to prove which method was the best. Next we will look at how the hyperparameters can be tuned, and what effect they have on the convergence.

### Hyper-parameter Tuning Examples

First, a brief comparison of learning rates with the standard gradient descent method. A high learning rate can lead to oscillations, as the algorithm repeatably oversteps the optimum. When this happens, the learning rate can be decreased. This reduces oscillations, but requires more iterations. In this case, a learning rate around 0.01 led to the second parameter converging.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (lr in c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1)) {
  gradient_control <- list(epsilon_decay = 1e-4)
  a_n <- c(0.01, 0.01)
  control <- list(
    ncores = 1, lr = lr, maxiters = c(1, 20),
    halfmax = 2, epsilon = 1e-8,
    deriv_epsilon = 1e-8, verbose = 4
  )
  e <- CoxRun(Cox(t0, t1, lung) ~ loglinear(dose, rand, 0) + m(), df,
    a_n = a_n, keep_constant = keep_constant,
    control = control, gradient_control = gradient_control
  )
  print(e)
}
```

Next, the momentum decay. The momentum decay term is helpful particularly when the standard method overshoots the solution. In this example, the momentum method was tested at a learning rate of 0.047 to induce oscillation. At a momentum decay of 0.0, we have the standard gradient descent and as we increase the momentum effect we reduce the oscillation. However, at too high of a decay value, we increase the oscillation.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (lr in c(0.0, 5.0, 7.0, 20.0)) {
  gradient_control <- list(momentum = TRUE, epsilon_decay = 1e-4, momentum_decay = lr)
  a_n <- c(0.01, 0.01)
  control <- list(
    ncores = 1, lr = 0.047, maxiters = c(1, 20),
    halfmax = 2, epsilon = 1e-8,
    deriv_epsilon = 1e-8, verbose = 4
  )
  e <- CoxRun(Cox(t0, t1, lung) ~ loglinear(dose, rand, 0) + m(), df,
    a_n = a_n, keep_constant = keep_constant,
    control = control, gradient_control = gradient_control
  )
  print(e)
}
```

Finally, we have the epsilon offset used in the adadelta method. In this example, if the offset is too low the change in parameter value per iteration is near zero, then as it is increased the algorithm converges faster until the estimate oscillates.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
for (lr in c(1e-8, 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2)) {
  gradient_control <- list(adadelta = TRUE, epsilon_decay = lr)
  a_n <- c(0.01, 0.01)
  control <- list(
    ncores = 1, lr = 0.75, maxiters = c(1, 20),
    halfmax = 2, epsilon = 1e-8,
    deriv_epsilon = 1e-8, verbose = 4
  )
  e <- CoxRun(Cox(t0, t1, lung) ~ loglinear(dose, rand, 0) + m(), df,
    a_n = a_n, keep_constant = keep_constant,
    control = control, gradient_control = gradient_control
  )
  print(e)
}
```
